design_detail: Four-page 'Analysis' article (critical narrative review) in The British Journal of Psychiatry, published online in 2020 (received 11 November 2019, accepted 23 April 2020), arguing that the licensing evidence for intranasal esketamine in 'treatment-resistant depression' did not establish efficacy and that safety signals were played down. Sources: the FDA review documents and Janssen's advisory-committee briefing document, published trial reports, commentaries (including Turner, 2019), news items, a Public Health England report and NICE draft guidance; three tables of deaths and adverse events taken from the FDA and Janssen documents. Background sections on ketamine's anaesthetic use, recreational use and harms cite one review (Morgan and Curran, 2012) for most of their statements. No search strategy. A corrigendum (Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618, online 2 July 2021) qualifies Table 1 and the statement on anaesthetic use. The PDF read is the online-first version, 'Page 1 of 4' to 'Page 4 of 4'.
can_establish: What the FDA and Janssen documents, as reproduced by the authors, show about deaths, worsening of depression and suicidality, common adverse events and bladder symptoms in the esketamine licensing programme, and the authors' arguments that the short-term trials were weak and the discontinuation trial confounded by withdrawal.
cannot_establish: That esketamine caused the deaths or suicides (the corrigendum states that Table 1 is not a randomized comparison and that exposure was larger and longer with esketamine); that relapse in the discontinuation trial was withdrawal (an untested hypothesis); or anything about ketamine's recreational harms beyond the secondary sources it cites.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The licensing programme as described: three 4-week efficacy trials, one discontinuation trial and one 60-week safety trial submitted by Janssen to the FDA (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF); 1861 participants exposed to esketamine and 486 to placebo in stage 2 and 3 trials up to 4 September 2018 (Table 1, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the authors chose the evidence.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen to support the critique. The regulatory documents are a defined source, but the background on recreational harms and several key arguments rest on secondary sources (one review, commentaries, a news item), and the case for efficacy made by the sponsor and the FDA is reported only where the authors rebut it.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited trials: intranasal esketamine against placebo (a nasal spray with an embittering agent) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as described by the authors: in the 4-week and discontinuation trials, esketamine 56 to 84 mg twice a week intranasally; in the 60-week safety study, weekly or fortnightly; the discontinuation trial enrolled people in stable remission after 16 weeks of esketamine (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF). The authors call the trial doses in line with recreational doses of ketamine and state that esketamine is twice as potent as ketamine, citing secondary sources (pp. 1–2).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed (the trials added esketamine to oral antidepressants, as the titles of the cited trial reports show).

comparison.controls: Placebo nasal spray in the trials; for deaths (Table 1), all placebo-exposed against all esketamine-exposed participants across stage 2 and 3 trials, including open-label periods, as the corrigendum states.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: MADRS change and relapse in the trials; Clinical Global Impression thresholds linked to MADRS change (from a separate equipercentile-linking study); Physician Withdrawal Checklist; adverse events, deaths, worsening of depression and suicidal ideas, blood pressure, bladder symptoms and cognitive impairment from the FDA and Janssen documents (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note the FDA's statement that adverse events were misclassified, under-reported and misrepresented, so Table 2 likely underestimates their incidence (Table 2 footnote, p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy judged by statistical significance across trials and by comparing the 4-point MADRS difference with change thresholds for individual patients; harm judged by counts of events in esketamine-exposed and placebo-exposed participants across different trial sets.

analysis.effect_sizes: As reproduced from the FDA and Janssen documents (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF): in the only positive 4-week trial, MADRS fell by 19.8 points with esketamine and 15.8 with placebo (baseline mean 37); deaths 6 of 1861 esketamine-exposed (0.3%; 3 suicides) against 0 of 486 placebo-exposed; worsening of suicidal ideas 5/570 (0.9%) against 2/432 (0.5%); worsening of depression 8/570 (1.4%) against 1/432 (0.2%); increased blood pressure 368/3646 (10.0%) against 15/432 (3.5%); in trials 3001 and 3002, dissociation 48.3% against 18.9%, dizziness 29.5% against 8.1%, nausea 28.9% against 8.6%, vertigo 22.5% against 2.7%, cystitis-suggestive events 10.7% against 2.7%. No confidence intervals or tests. Corrigendum (publisher HTML, p. 618): in the long-term safety study, 114 of 784 (14.5%) reported treatment-emergent suicidal ideation; post-marketing reports in the first 12 months gave reporting odds 24 times higher for suicidal ideation and 6 times higher for completed suicide than for other drugs, from a cited disproportionality analysis.
analysis.selective_reporting: Arguments are one-sided by design. Table 1 compared deaths across unequal, partly open-label exposure without saying so until the corrigendum. Table 2 uses different denominators for different rows (570 against 3646 esketamine-exposed). Several statements are attributed to secondary sources that do not contain them (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The figures reproduced from the regulatory documents show one significant 4-week trial out of three with a 4-point MADRS difference, a discontinuation trial in an enriched group whose significance depended on one site, six deaths (three suicides) among esketamine-exposed participants and none among the fewer placebo-exposed participants, small excesses of worsening depression and suicidal ideas, and common acute adverse effects (dissociation in about half in two 4-week trials, against about a fifth with placebo), with bladder symptoms in about a fifth in the 60-week open-label study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary states that the licensing trials "did not establish efficacy" and that safety signals, including deaths, suicides and bladder damage, were "minimised" (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the conclusion speaks of patients as unwitting guinea pigs in an unregulated experiment (p. 3). Gaps: (1) the deaths are presented as occurring only in those assigned to esketamine, without saying that Table 1 pools open-label and placebo-controlled periods with much larger and longer esketamine exposure; the authors' own corrigendum (2021) concedes that no causal inference can be drawn from it; (2) withdrawal as the explanation for relapse after stopping esketamine is the authors' argument, and withdrawal as the explanation for the suicides comes from a commentary; neither was tested; (3) the 4-point between-group difference is compared with change thresholds for individual patients, which are not the same quantity; (4) several statements are attributed to Turner (2019), whose Comment does not make them. The criticisms of the trial evidence that come from the FDA's own documents (one positive short-term trial, enrichment, the outlier site, unblinding) are documented.

timeline.event: Daly et al.: phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine (this round's first-pass card sc_daly_2018).
Turner: Comment with seven concerns about the efficacy evidence and the FDA approval, including the outlier-site re-analysis that this article cites.
Schatzberg: commentary cited here for the timing of the three suicides and the possibility of a withdrawal reaction (not read).
NICE draft guidance (January) recommending against esketamine for treatment-resistant depression, as described here; this article published online.

Corrigendum (Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618, online 2 July 2021): Table 1 pools phase 2 and phase 3 data including open-label periods, is not a randomized comparison and allows no causal inference; adds long-term safety-study and post-marketing data on suicidality; qualifies the statement on anaesthetic use.
Dean et al.: Cochrane review of randomized trials of ketamine, esketamine and other glutamate modulators in unipolar depression (this round's first-pass card sc_dean_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The efficacy criticisms overlap with Turner (2019) and rest on the same FDA documents; the safety criticisms rely on non-randomized counts, which the authors' corrigendum acknowledges. Randomized long-term safety data remain the gap both articles identify.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: J.M. (Joanna Moncrieff) is co-chairperson of the Critical Psychiatry Network; ICMJE disclosure forms are in the online supplementary material (Declaration of interest, p. 4 of the online-first PDF), which was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Division of Psychiatry, University College London, and North East London Foundation Trust. M.A.H. wrote the article; J.M. edited it and supervised (Author contributions, p. 4). The Critical Psychiatry Network position is relevant to a critique of a new psychiatric drug. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the article.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of esketamine lasting a year or more, with placebo or active comparator arms of equal exposure, pre-specified collection of deaths, suicidal ideation and behaviour, urinary and cognitive outcomes, and a discontinuation design that tapers treatment and measures withdrawal symptoms separately from relapse.

domains.note: No search or criteria; regulatory documents mixed with commentaries, news items and one review chosen by the authors.

The trials are appraised critically (unblinding, enrichment, outlier site, possible withdrawal confounding), but the sources for the harm claims are not, and non-randomized death counts were presented as a comparison until the corrigendum.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No studies by the authors are cited.

The withdrawal explanations for relapse and for the suicides are presented beside the data without being marked as untested; the Summary's wording goes beyond what the tables show; several statements are attributed to a source that does not contain them.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against esketamine's efficacy and safety (the sponsor's and the FDA's case is under-represented)
domains.note: The FDA's reasons for approval and its assessment of the deaths are reported only to be rebutted; positive data (the significant trial, the overall relapse result) are mentioned only with their weaknesses.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative critique (METHODS §5.3). The article usefully brings together regulatory data that are hard to find (deaths, worsening of depression and suicidality, common adverse events, bladder symptoms) and states the main weaknesses of the efficacy evidence; but its selection is unsystematic and one-sided, its central safety table needed a corrigendum to say it allows no causal inference, and several attributions to secondary sources do not check out. It may be cited for the counts it reproduces from the FDA and Janssen documents (with their denominators and the corrigendum's caveat) and as a published critique; it may not be cited for esketamine causing deaths or suicides, for withdrawal as the cause of relapse, or for ketamine's recreational harms, which must be cited to primary studies.

key_findings.finding: The authors' Summary: licensing trials did not establish efficacy (two negative trials, one statistically significant but clinically uncertain, and a flawed discontinuation trial accepted against FDA precedent), and safety signals including deaths, suicides and bladder damage were minimised.

Janssen submitted five studies to the FDA: three 4-week efficacy trials, one discontinuation trial and one 60-week safety trial; in the 4-week and discontinuation trials esketamine was given at 56 to 84 mg twice a week intranasally; only one of the three short-term trials showed a statistically significant difference from placebo.
key_findings.locator: Evidence submitted to the FDA, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In the only positive 4-week trial, the MADRS (0 to 60, baseline mean 37) fell by 19.8 points with esketamine and 15.8 with placebo, a 4-point difference; the authors compare this with a 7 to 9 point change corresponding to 'minimally improved' and 16 to 17 points to 'much improved' on the Clinical Global Impression scale, and note that dissociation would have unmasked participants.
key_findings.note: Turner (2019, p. 1 of its online-first PDF), citing FDA slide 24, gives 20.8 and 16.8 for the same trial; both give a 4-point difference. The CGI thresholds describe change in individual patients, not differences between group means.

key_findings.finding: Discontinuation trial: people in stable remission after 16 weeks of esketamine were randomized to continue or stop; the authors argue that withdrawal effects could be mistaken for relapse, noting that Physician Withdrawal Checklist scores are not reported, that 48.7% of relapses occurred in the first 4 weeks after stopping, that the FDA observed the placebo relapse rate moving closer to esketamine week by week, and that higher dissociation scores on treatment were correlated with shorter time to relapse.

The FDA raised the concern that the discontinuation trial's result was driven by one site in Poland, where all 16 placebo participants relapsed, against 33% in the placebo arm elsewhere (printed as n = 81); without that site the P value changes from 0.012 to 0.48 (citing Turner's Comment, reference 18).
key_findings.note: The n = 81 for the placebo arm elsewhere does not fit; see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: Six deaths occurred in the licensing trials, all among esketamine-exposed participants: 3 suicides, 1 fatal motor vehicle accident (a motorcycle accident 26 hours after a dose), 1 myocardial infarction (6 days after a dose) and 1 death from acute respiratory and cardiac failure (5 days after a dose, in a person with risk factors); Table 1 gives 6/1861 (0.3%) esketamine-exposed against 0/486 placebo-exposed participants in stage 2 and 3 trials up to 4 September 2018. The FDA judged these deaths difficult to consider drug-related.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The authors' corrigendum (2021) states that Table 1 pools phase 2 and phase 3 data including open-label periods, is not a randomized comparison, and that more and longer esketamine exposure may partly explain the difference.

key_findings.finding: The three suicides occurred 4, 12 and 20 days after the last dose; two of the three had shown no suicidal ideas at study entry or at the last visit (no data for the third); the FDA attributed the deaths to the severity of the underlying illness and accepted Janssen's view that they were not drug-related; a cited commentary argued they might fit a severe withdrawal reaction.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: One esketamine participant had a non-fatal cerebral haemorrhage and five more in the esketamine arms had non-fatal motor vehicle accidents.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, continued on p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Selected adverse events (Table 2; 4-week trials 3001, 3002, 3005 and discontinuation trial 3003 unless stated): worsening of suicidal ideas 2/432 (0.5%) with placebo against 5/570 (0.9%) with esketamine; worsening of depression 1/432 (0.2%) against 8/570 (1.4%); non-fatal motor vehicle accidents 0 against 5 (denominators not reported); increased blood pressure 15/432 (3.5%) against 368/3646 (10.0%), the latter denominators being participants in completed stage 3 studies. The FDA noted misclassification, under-reporting and misrepresentation of adverse events, so these figures likely underestimate incidence.
key_findings.note: The text gives six, not eight, participants with worsening depression; see reporting issue 1.

key_findings.finding: Most common adverse events in the 4-week trials 3001 and 3002 (placebo against esketamine, % of exposed): dissociation 18.9 against 48.3; dizziness 8.1 against 29.5; nausea 8.6 against 28.9; headache 18.0 against 19.7; sedation 9.9 against 23.1; anxiety 7.7 against 13.3; vertigo 2.7 against 22.5; hypoaesthesia 1.8 against 12.7; blood pressure increase 1.4 against 10.7; vomiting 1.4 against 11.3; cystitis-suggestive adverse events 2.7 against 10.7.

Signs of bladder irritation (urinary tract infections, pain, discomfort, cystitis, nocturia) occurred in esketamine participants; in the 60-week study with weekly or fortnightly dosing, a fifth reported bladder effects, and some cognitive impairment was detected among older participants; the FDA argued that without a comparison arm these effects could not be attributed to esketamine.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: When licensing esketamine, the FDA required a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy because of sedation, dissociation and diversion: administration in a healthcare setting with monitoring for at least 2 hours.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The MHRA licensed esketamine; NICE's draft guidance of January 2020 recommended against its use for treatment-resistant depression, citing a lack of evidence that it was more effective than existing treatments including psychological treatment, a lack of long-term evidence and unlikely cost-effectiveness.
key_findings.locator: MHRA and NICE reviews of esketamine, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Corrigendum (2021): Table 1 combines phase 2 data (open-label and placebo-controlled periods) with phase 3 data (placebo-controlled efficacy studies, a maintenance-of-effect study and a long-term open-label safety study), so it is not a randomized comparison and permits no definitive causal inference; more patients were exposed to esketamine, and for longer, which may be one reason for more suicides in that group. The corrigendum adds that in the long-term safety study 114 of 784 (14.5%) esketamine patients reported treatment-emergent suicidal ideation and 6 attempted suicide besides the one completed suicide, and that a disproportionality analysis of US post-marketing reports in the first 12 months found 64 reports of suicidal ideation, 11 completed suicides and 6 attempts, with reporting odds 24-fold (ideation) and 6-fold (completed suicide) those of other drugs. It also states that ketamine is not used routinely as an anaesthetic in high-income countries such as the UK but is used more often in low-income countries.
key_findings.locator: Corrigendum, doi 10.1192/bjp.2021.40, Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618: 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The post-marketing figures are spontaneous reports, which cannot give incidence; the corrigendum cites Wajs et al. (2020) and Gastaldon et al. (2020), not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says six participants (1.4%) in the esketamine group of the short-term trials became more depressed, against one on placebo (0.2%), while Table 2 gives 8/570 (1.4%) for worsening of depression. Editors' calculation: 6 of 570 is 1.1%, so the text's count and percentage disagree, and the percentage matches Table 2's eight.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of esketamine participants with worsening depression is 8 (Table 2) or 6 (text); claims should use the table and say the text differs. The corrigendum does not address it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives increased blood pressure as 368/3646 with esketamine, footnoted as participants in completed stage 3 studies, while Table 1 gives 1861 participants exposed to esketamine in all stage 2 and stage 3 trials up to September 2018, and the other rows of Table 2 use 570.
reporting_issues.consequence: 3646 cannot be a count of esketamine-exposed participants on the article's own figures; the 10.0% rate and its comparison with 3.5% on placebo (432) should not be cited from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The placebo arm at the sites other than the outlier site is given as n = 81. Editors' cross-check with Turner (2019), whose figure the cited P values come from: 86 placebo participants overall and 16 at the outlier site leave 70; Turner's P values are reproduced with 23 of 70 placebo relapses (33%) and 22 of 81 esketamine relapses, so 81 is the esketamine arm at those sites, a label swapped in Turner's figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 33% relapse rate in the placebo arm elsewhere is right, but its denominator is 70, not 81.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements are cited to reference 18 (Turner, 2019) that its Comment does not contain: the phrase that the FDA requires two positive trials each convincing on its own, the statement that the FDA loosened its rules to accept a discontinuation trial (and the Summary's 'against FDA precedent'), and the conclusion that a 4-point difference has doubtful clinical relevance. Editors' check against turner_2019, read in full: none of these appears; Turner refers to the FDA requirement for substantial evidence of effectiveness.
reporting_issues.consequence: These points must be cited to the FDA documents or other sources, not to Turner (2019) through this article.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that dissociation was reported by the majority of participants, and later by half, while Table 3 gives 48.3% with esketamine in trials 3001 and 3002.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; claims should give 48.3% (against 18.9% with placebo).

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 6, the source of the figure that 3.1% of 16- to 24-year-olds in England and Wales used ketamine in 2017–2018, is cited as an item in Computer Fraud and Security (2018), not as an Office for National Statistics publication; and the trial showing rapid-onset antidepressant effects within 2 hours is cited to a pharmacology review (reference 13), not to a trial.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prevalence figure must be taken from the Crime Survey for England and Wales directly; the background section cannot be used to trace primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 and the text present the six deaths as occurring only among participants assigned to esketamine, without saying that the data pool open-label and placebo-controlled periods with unequal exposure; the authors' corrigendum supplies this and states that no causal inference can be drawn.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about deaths in esketamine trials must carry the corrigendum's caveat and cannot present 6/1861 against 0/486 as a randomized comparison.

Read in full: Summary, all sections, Tables 1 to 3 (checked on the rendered pages at 150 dpi), author details, contributions, declaration of interest and references; the online ICMJE forms were not read. Corrigendum read as publisher full text (HTML), The British Journal of Psychiatry, Cambridge Core page reached from https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.2021.40 (title confirmed; Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618, published online 2 July 2021), in the app's browser on 31 October 2026.
